      <content name="FullSummary">What is <span class="qt4">lung</span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span>?<p><span class="qt4">Lung</span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer is cancer</span></span> that forms in tissues of the <span class="qt4">lung</span>, usually in the cells that line the air passages. It is the leading cause of <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span> death in both men and women.</p><p>There are two main types: small cell <span class="qt4">lung</span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span> and <span class="qt3">non-small cell</span> <span class="qt4">lung</span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span>. These two types grow differently and are treated differently. <span class="qt3">Non-small cell</span> <span class="qt4">lung</span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span> is the more common type.</p>Who is more likely to develop <span class="qt4">lung</span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span>?<p>Anyone can develop <span class="qt4">lung</span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span>, but certain factors raise your risk of getting it:</p><ul><li>Smoking. This is the most important risk factor for <span class="qt4">lung</span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span>. Tobacco smoking causes about 9 out of 10 cases of <span class="qt4">lung</span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span> in men and about 8 out of 10 cases of <span class="qt4">lung</span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span> in women. The more years you smoke and the more cigarettes you smoke each day, the more your risk goes up.  Your risk is also greater if you smoke a lot and drink alcohol every day or take beta carotene supplements. If you have quit smoking, your risk will be lower than if you had kept smoking. But you will still have a higher risk than people who never smoked.</li><li>Secondhand smoke, which is the combination of the smoke that comes from a cigarette and the smoke breathed out by a smoker. When you breathe in secondhand smoke, you are exposed to the same <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span>-causing agents as smokers, although in smaller amounts.</li><li>A family history of <span class="qt4">lung</span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span>.</li><li>Being exposed to asbestos, arsenic, chromium, beryllium, nickel, soot, or tar in the workplace.</li><li>Being exposed to radiation, for example from:
	<ul><li>Radiation therapy to the breast or chest</li><li>Radon in the home or workplace</li><li>Certain imaging tests such as CT scans</li></ul>
</li><li>HIV infection. Your risk is higher if you have HIV. However, smoking rates are higher in people who have HIV, so it's not clear whether the increased risk is from the HIV infection or from smoking.</li><li>Air pollution. Studies show that living in areas with higher levels of air pollution increases your risk of <span class="qt4">lung</span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span>.</li></ul>What are the symptoms of <span class="qt4">lung</span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span>?<p><span class="qt4">Lung</span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span> may not cause any signs or symptoms until the <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span> is advanced. Sometimes the <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span> is found during a chest x-ray done for another condition.</p><p>The symptoms of <span class="qt4">lung</span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span> may include:</p><ul><li>Chest pain or discomfort</li><li>A cough that doesn't go away or gets worse over time</li><li>Coughing up blood</li><li>Trouble breathing</li><li>Wheezing</li><li>Hoarseness</li><li>Loss of appetite</li><li>Weight loss for no known reason</li><li>Feeling very tired</li><li>Trouble swallowing</li><li>Swelling in the face and/or veins in the neck</li></ul>How is <span class="qt4">lung</span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span> diagnosed?<p>To find out if you have <span class="qt4">lung</span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span>, your health care provider:</p><ul><li>Will take your medical history, which includes asking about your symptoms</li><li>Will ask about your family history</li><li>Will do a physical exam</li><li>May order certain imaging tests, such as a chest x-ray or chest CT scan</li><li>May order lab tests, including tests of your blood and sputum</li><li>May do a procedure to take a biopsy of the <span class="qt4">lung</span></li></ul><p>If you do have <span class="qt4">lung</span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span>, your provider will do other tests to find out if it has spread through the <span class="qt4">lungs</span>, lymph nodes, and the rest of the body. This is called staging. Knowing the type and stage of <span class="qt4">lung</span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span> you have helps your provider decide what kind of treatment you need.</p><p>If you have small-cell <span class="qt4">lung</span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span>, your provider may also do genetic testing to look for certain gene changes (variants) in your <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span> cells. The results of the testing may help guide treatment.</p>What are the treatments for <span class="qt4">lung</span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span>?<p>For most patients with <span class="qt4">lung</span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span>, current treatments do not cure the <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span>.</p><p>Your treatment will depend on which type of <span class="qt4">lung</span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span> you have, how far it has spread, your overall health, and other factors. You may get more than one type of treatment.</p><p>The treatments for small cell <span class="qt4">lung</span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span> may include:</p><ul><li>Surgery.</li><li>Chemotherapy.</li><li>Radiation therapy.</li><li>Immunotherapy.</li><li>Laser therapy, which uses a laser beam to kill <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span> cells.</li><li>Endoscopic stent placement. An endoscope is a thin, tube-like instrument used to look at tissues inside the body. It may be used to put in a device called a stent. The stent helps to open an airway that has been blocked by abnormal tissue.</li></ul><p>The treatments for <span class="qt3">non-small cell</span> <span class="qt4">lung</span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span> may include:</p><ul><li>Surgery.</li><li>Radiation therapy.</li><li>Chemotherapy.</li><li>Targeted therapy, which uses drugs or other substances that attack specific <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span> cells with less harm to normal cells.</li><li>Immunotherapy.</li><li>Laser therapy.</li><li>Photodynamic therapy (PDT), which uses a medicine and a certain type of laser light to kill <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span> cells.</li><li>Cryosurgery, which uses an instrument to freeze and destroy abnormal tissue.</li><li>Electrocautery, a treatment that uses a probe or needle heated by an electric current to destroy abnormal tissue.</li></ul>Can <span class="qt4">lung</span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span> be prevented?<p>Avoiding the risk factors may help prevent <span class="qt4">lung</span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span>. For example, you can:</p><ul><li>Quit smoking. And if you don't smoke, don't start.</li><li>Lower your exposure to hazardous substances at work.</li><li>Lower your exposure to radon. Radon tests can show whether your home has high levels of radon. You can buy a test kit yourself or hire a professional to do the test.</li></ul><p>NIH: National <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">Cancer</span></span> Institute</p></content>
